text:
Does the Williamson-van der Mark confined-photon electron imply anything about chemical bonding, or is the phase resemblance only an analogy?

The 1997 Williamson and van der Mark paper, “Is the electron a photon with toroidal topology?”, postulates one thing: a circularly polarized photon can self-confine on a closed path of one Compton wavelength (lambda\_C ≈ 2.43 × 10\^-12 m). One full field twist makes the electric field point radially, which they identify with electron or positron charge, plus a magnetic moment and spin 1/2. The paper stops at the single electron. It has no molecule and no bond.

Molecular orbital theory explains bonds by phase. In-phase overlap of atomic orbitals lowers the energy (bonding); out-of-phase overlap raises it (antibonding). Bond order is (n\_bonding - n\_antibonding) / 2. The toroidal model also lives by phase matching, but the phase is internal to one photon, not a relation between orbitals on two atoms.

The open question is whether that resemblance can be turned into a bonding theory. Call it a confined-photon bonding theory only as a proposal, not as a result in the paper. Two loops near two nuclei would need an interaction energy E(R, phi) with a minimum at the observed bond length and depth. For H2 that is about 0.74 angstrom and 4.52 eV.

One constraint: the electron rest energy stays 511 keV inside a bond, so the Compton loop cannot simply stretch out to bond length. The open piece, if any, is a small overlap energy E(R, phi) that has not been written down.

Paper: J. G. Williamson and M. B. van der Mark, Annales de la Fondation Louis de Broglie 22, 133 (1997).

text:
How accurate is my explanation of entropy?

I actually had to learn about the basics of entropy for AP Biology, but I ended up going down a huge rabbit hole trying to understand it and now I'm genuinely interested in it. I wrote down an explanation of entropy (pasted below) for my own comprehension and I wanted to know what I might need to correct or add on to make my understanding of entropy more accurate. Further explanation on this stuff would be much appreciated!!

\--

Entropy can simply be defined as a measurement of the disorder of the universe. But what does any of that actually mean?

Think of the universe as a box. When the Big Bang happened and introduced a bunch of individual galaxies, it was like putting a bunch of colored balls in the box.

Increasing the amount of stuff in the box changes the amount of configurations the balls can be in. (The amount of configurations can be referred to as “states”, or possible states of matter. Increasing the amount of matter, just like increasing the number of balls, leads to an increased amount of possible states the matter can be in.)

Entropy is a demonstration of the probability that the balls inside the box will exist in a disorganized or random “state” rather than an organized one. It’s possible, of course, that the balls will align in an organized fashion, but the probability of this occurring is far less likely than the probability that the balls will be disorganized.

High entropy refers to naturally occurring processes that lead to more disorder, or disorganization, in the overall universe. These processes have high entropy specifically because they happen naturally, without any added energy. Examples are water flowing downstream, or ice melting.

If we were comparing ice and water, we would say water has higher entropy than ice because its molecules are free floating and move around quite a bit, while ice’s molecules are fixed in place and barely move at all. There’s more possible states the water molecules can be in, while ice has less possible states—water molecules have more randomness, which leads to higher entropy.

In the context of chemical reactions, the entropy or disorder of the universe inc as chemical reactions transfer or transform energy. For example, eating mac and cheese (im hungry). The mac and cheese’s energy is converted to different forms of energy once eaten and digested so the body can carry out biological processes. Some of this energy is released as thermal energy, or heat, which introduces more molecules into the universe that changes the possible states of matter within the universe, thus increasing its entropy.

So, to put it simply: entropy measures the randomness or disorder of the universe, which increases as chemical reactions occur. Typing this shit out rn is currently increasing the entropy of the universe

It is said that if our universe had possessed even slightly more mass at the moment of the Big Bang, it would have already collapsed in on itself, and we would not be here today; conversely, if it had possessed slightly less mass, it would have simply dispersed.

So, what magnitude of excess or deficit would cause such an outcome? Why do we face this issue?



It’s said a deviation of just one part in 10⁶⁰ from the critical density would have caused our universe to either collapse or disperse long ago. This represents an extraordinary level of precision; considering the observable universe—where the total mass (including dark matter and energy) is 10⁵⁴ kg—the precision required at the time of the Big Bang was on the order of 10⁵⁴/10⁶⁰. This equates to 1/10⁶ kg, or one milligram.

In other words, had the mass of our universe at the time of the Big Bang differed by even the weight of a single grain of sand—whether in excess or deficit—it would have either collapsed in on itself or dispersed long ago.
